issues.legal_issue: The amount of mesne profits may be determined from the whole evidentiary record and need not be confined to figures in the books maintained by the party in possession.
material_facts: The claim concerned profits from the wrongful use of a co-owner’s share in a tea estate, and liability to pay mesne profits was not disputed.
The High Court considered the accounts, a commissioner’s report, and other evidence in assessing the amount.
The Supreme Court found no reason to reappreciate the material or disturb the High Court’s determination.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s determination of the amount of mesne profits was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 2(12) of the Code of Civil Procedure, mesne profits include profits actually received or which might with ordinary diligence have been received by a person in wrongful possession, together with interest. A court may apply recognised valuation methods and is not bound to accept figures based only on unproved books of account. The Supreme Court declined to reappreciate the material supporting the High Court’s finding.

predicates.final_decree_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging the determination of mesne profits in a final decree.
predicates.mesne_profit_liability_undisputed: The party challenging the decree did not dispute liability to pay mesne profits, but disputed their amount.
predicates.high_court_assessed_relevant_evidence: The High Court assessed the amount using the available accounts, a commissioner’s material, and other relevant evidence.

issues.definition: When a final-decree appeal concerns only the amount of undisputed mesne-profit liability and the High Court assessed relevant evidence, the amount determined by the High Court is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: The interest award in a suit instituted before the relevant procedural amendment is governed by the earlier interest rules, and a non-commercial claim for mesne profits does not justify interest at commercial bank rates.
material_facts: The suit was instituted before the amendment to the provision governing interest.
The plaintiff originally claimed interest at six per cent and later obtained permission to amend the claim to seek a higher rate for mesne profits.
The High Court awarded interest at varying commercial bank rates, although the claim concerned a co-owner’s share in property and was not a commercial transaction.
The preliminary decree concerning the partnership accounts had awarded six per cent interest and was not challenged on that point.
issues.conclusion: Interest on both the accounts decree and the mesne-profits decree was limited to six per cent; pre-decree interest on mesne profits was to be at a reasonable rate, which the Court fixed at six per cent in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Unamended Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs suits instituted before the amendment, by virtue of Section 97(2)(e) of the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 1976. Under that version, post-decree interest could not exceed six per cent, while pre-decree interest was for the court to set at a reasonable rate. The Court relied on M/s Shree Bharat Laxmi Wool Store, Panipat v. Punjab National Bank for the non-application of the amendment to earlier suits. It also held that interest on mesne profits for retention of a co-owner’s property was not based on a commercial transaction.

predicates.interest_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging an award of interest in a civil decree.
predicates.suit_predates_interest_amendment: The suit was instituted before the applicable change to the rules governing interest took effect.
predicates.claim_is_noncommercial: The interest claim arose from retention and use of a co-owner’s property rather than a commercial transaction.

issues.definition: If an interest appeal concerns a suit instituted before the applicable change and a non-commercial claim, the interest award is limited to the permissible rate.

issues.legal_issue: A court that allows an amendment to pleadings must give the opposing party a fair opportunity to answer and contest the amended plea before deciding it.
material_facts: The High Court allowed an amendment seeking a higher interest rate while disposing of the appeal on the same day.
No amended pleading was filed and the defendants were not given an opportunity to contest the amended claim.
The decree awarded interest at a rate exceeding even the rate sought in the permitted amendment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s award of interest beyond the original claim was illegal and unsustainable because the amended plea had not been contested and was decided without a fair opportunity to respond.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings to determine the real questions in controversy, but the opposing party must be allowed to respond and the court must decide the contested issue. J. Jermons v. Aliammal held that a new plea cannot be raised without amendment, a reasonable opportunity for further pleadings, and an opportunity to adduce evidence.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.amended_plea_allowed: The court permitted a party to amend a plea in its pleadings.
predicates.opposing_party_not_given_opportunity: The opposing party was not given a reasonable opportunity to answer the amended plea and contest it.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal involves an allowed amended plea that the opposing party had no opportunity to contest, the plea is not enforced without that opportunity.

issues.legal_issue: Dismissal of a petition for special leave to appeal does not affirm the challenged judgment or prevent review after leave to appeal has been granted.
material_facts: A petition for special leave challenging the earlier decree had previously been dismissed.
The present proceedings were full appeals after leave to appeal had been granted.
The respondent argued that the dismissal of the earlier petition prevented reconsideration of the interest ruling.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court could examine the legality and correctness of the challenged judgment in the full appeals notwithstanding the earlier dismissal of the special-leave petition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, dismissal of a special-leave petition does not reverse, modify, or affirm the challenged judgment and does not make that judgment res judicata. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala.

predicates.full_appeal_after_leave_granted: The proceeding was a full appeal heard after leave to appeal had been granted.
predicates.earlier_special_leave_petition_dismissed: A petition for special leave challenging the judgment had previously been dismissed.

issues.definition: When a full appeal follows the grant of leave despite an earlier dismissal of a special-leave petition, appellate review remains available.

issues.legal_issue: Interest on mesne profits that accrue over successive years must be calculated on the amount attributable to each year rather than on the entire accumulated amount from the outset.
material_facts: The mesne profits accrued over a series of years.
The High Court calculated interest on the total amount from the beginning, although the yearly amounts became due successively.
The Supreme Court held that the calculation should reflect the year-by-year accrual of mesne profits.
issues.conclusion: Interest on mesne profits was to be calculated on the amount due at the end of each successive year, with interest on the final lump-sum amount running from the date specified by the Court.
issues.legal_principle: Where mesne profits accrue year by year, interest is calculated on the amount that had become due at the end of each successive year; it is not calculated on the total accumulated amount from the beginning.

predicates.mesne_profit_decree_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning a decree for mesne profits.
predicates.mesne_profits_accrue_successively: The mesne profits became due in successive periods rather than as one amount due at the outset.

issues.definition: When a mesne-profit decree appeal concerns profits that accrue successively, interest is calculated on the amounts attributable to successive annual accruals.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who accepts workers transferred with a partitioned part of an estate and later sells that part cannot reopen a claim for reimbursement of gratuity paid to those workers.
material_facts: The plaintiff insisted on receiving trained workers along with the portion of the tea estate allotted to her.
The plaintiff was aware of her obligations concerning those workers when she took them.
She later sold the portion of the estate that had been allotted to her and sought reimbursement for gratuity paid to the workers.
issues.conclusion: The claim for reimbursement of gratuity was rejected and could not be reopened at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: A person who knowingly takes workers along with property allotted on partition assumes the obligations associated with those workers; a claim for reimbursement of their gratuity cannot be reopened on the facts of this case.

predicates.partition_appeal: The proceeding included an appeal concerning the consequences of partitioning property.
predicates.claimant_accepted_workers_with_property: The claimant insisted on and accepted workers along with the property allotted to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_knew_worker_obligations: The claimant was aware of obligations concerning those workers when accepting them.

issues.definition: When a partition appeal concerns a claimant who accepted workers with property while aware of their obligations, the claim for gratuity reimbursement is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: A deceased partner’s share of partnership goodwill may be valued and included in the assets to be accounted for on dissolution.
material_facts: The partnership had conducted business continuously for many years.
The deceased partner held a share in the firm, and the plaintiff claimed the deceased partner’s share of its goodwill.
The courts below valued goodwill using the firm’s profits over the preceding years and gave reasons for including it.
Evidence supported the firm’s continuing business and reputation.
issues.conclusion: The award of the plaintiff’s share of the firm’s goodwill was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Goodwill is generally an asset of a partnership to be valued and distributed on dissolution. It may represent the advantage, reputation, and business connection associated with the continuing undertaking. The Court referred to Inland Revenue Commissioner v. Muller & Co. and the discussion of partnership goodwill in Halsbury’s Laws of England; it found no infirmity in valuing goodwill by reference to profits over a period of years.

predicates.partnership_accounting_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the accounting and distribution of partnership assets.
predicates.partnership_business_continued: The partnership had carried on its business continuously over a period of time.
predicates.goodwill_supported_by_evidence: Evidence and the courts’ assessment supported the existence and valuation of the partnership’s goodwill.

issues.definition: When a partnership-accounting appeal concerns a continuing business and evidence supports goodwill, the deceased partner’s share of goodwill is included.

issues.legal_issue: A debt shown by the evidence to have been adjusted and no longer outstanding cannot be deducted again from a deceased partner’s share in the partnership accounts.
material_facts: The appellants sought to deduct a debt allegedly owed by the deceased partner’s separate company to the partnership.
The trial court found that the debt had been adjusted in the partnership accounts.
The record included evidence of the adjustment, later accounts that no longer showed the separate company as a debtor, and evidence that no payment demand was made.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the debt had already been adjusted was upheld, and no further deduction was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: A court may uphold an accounting finding based on the evidence that a debt was previously adjusted and was no longer subsisting; the Court accepted the lower courts’ reasoning on the accounting record.

predicates.partnership_accounting_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the calculation of a partner’s share in partnership accounts.
predicates.debt_previously_adjusted: The evidence showed that the disputed debt had already been adjusted in the accounts.
predicates.later_accounts_show_no_outstanding_debt: Later accounts did not record the alleged debtor as owing the debt, and no demand for payment was made.

issues.definition: When a partnership-accounting appeal shows that a debt was previously adjusted and later accounts show it was no longer outstanding, the debt is not deducted again.
